10      A.    I hold a PhD and a Master of Science in economics from the W.P. Carey School

11            of Business at Arizona State University. I also earned a Bachelor of Arts in

12            economics and mathematics from Arizona State University. I served as a utility

18            California (“TURN”) from 2023-2024. At the Oregon Legislature, I was the

19            Revenue Economist responsible for energy, natural resources, forestry,

20            property, and telecommunications from 2017-2023. My Witness Qualifications

21            Statement is attached as Exhibit JLM-1.

10             Q.    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

11             A.    The purpose of my testimony is to respond to the Company’s rate case filed in

12                   this docket on November 20, 2025, along with supporting and supplemental

13                   testimony, and to provide recommendations to assist the Commission in its

14                   thorough and careful consideration of the Company’s proposed rate increase,

15                   including the impact on customers.

1    Q.   IN SETTING THE REVENUE REQUIREMENT, RETURN ON EQUITY

2         (“ROE”), ALLOCATION, AND RATE DESIGN CHANGES FOR THE

3         COMPANY, SHOULD THE COMMISSION CONSIDER THE IMPACT

4         OF THE PROPOSED RATE INCREASE ON BUSINESS CUSTOMERS?

5    A.   Yes. Electricity is a significant operating cost for retailers such as Walmart.

6         When electric rates increase, the increased cost to retailers can put pressure on

7         consumer prices and on the other expenses required by a business to operate.

8         The Commission should thoroughly and carefully consider the impact on

 9        customers in examining the requested revenue requirement and ROE, in

10        addition to all other facets of this case, to ensure that any increase in the

11        Company’s rates is the minimum amount necessary to provide safe, adequate,

12        and reliable service, while also providing SPS the opportunity to recover its

13        reasonable and prudent costs and earn a reasonable return on its investment.

14   Q.   PLEASE SUMMARIZE WALMART’S RECOMMENDATIONS TO

15        THE COMMISSION.

16   A.   Walmart’s recommendations to the Commission are as follows:

17        1) The Commission should closely examine the Company’s proposed revenue

18           requirement increase and the associated ROE especially in light of:

19           a. The customer impact of the resulting revenue requirement increase;

 6         nationwide, as discussed in more detail below, that do not support the

15         test year for the calculation of the load factor used in the A&E 4CP

16         allocator; and

17      b. The Commission should allocate the Company’s fixed wind production

18         capacity costs using the same A&E 4CP allocator as recommended for

19         the Company’s steam and other generation assets.

 6      requirement, Walmart recommends that the rates for LP Secondary be set

18      non-aggregated load at point of service or an NAICS primary code of 5182

19      – Data Processing, hosting and related services be required to take service

20      on the newly created VLL schedule.

 1          Q.       WHAT IS THE FIRST ISSUE?

 2          A.       The first issue is that the Company proposes to use a system load factor for the

 3                   A&E 4CP allocator based on the system peak demands during the four peak

 4                   months of June through September. 20

 5          Q.       WHY IS THIS AN ISSUE?

 6          A.       Calculating the system load factor base on the four peak months instead of a

 7                   single peak reduces the level of system peak used in the calculation and

 8                   artificially increases the system load factor. This, in turn, increases the amount

 9                   of production demand costs that are allocated in the energy portion of the A&E

10                   allocator and inappropriately shifts costs to higher load factor customer classes.

11          Q.       WHAT IS WALMART’S RECOMMENDATION ON THIS ISSUE?

12          A.       The Commission should approve the use of SPS’s single peak for the test year

13                   for the calculation of the load factor used in the A&E 4CP allocator.

14          Q.       WHAT IS THE SECOND ISSUE?

15          A.       The second issue is the proposed use of an energy allocator for the production

16                   demand costs of the Sagamore and Hale wind resources.

 4          Q.      DO A UTILITY’S FIXED PRODUCTION CAPACITY COSTS

 5                  CHANGE WITH CHANGES IN THE AMOUNT OF ELECTRICITY

 6                  GENERATED?

 7          A.      No. The utility’s fixed production capacity costs do not change with changes in

 8                  the amount of electricity generated. For example, if a baseload unit is not

 9                  dispatched and produces no energy, the fixed costs are not avoided by the utility

10                  or customers. Generation units can be built and operated for different reasons,

12                  generation unit is operated does not change the fact that the fixed costs are, in

13                  fact, fixed, and should be treated as such in the production capacity cost

14                  allocation.

 8   A.   Basing the allocation of production capacity cost on the utility’s system peak

15        fixed cost to meet that demand, but because one class uses more kWh than the

17        kWh. Additionally, use of an energy allocator implies that the generation plant

18        to which that allocator is applied has no fixed cost, which is plainly not the case.

19   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR UNDERSTANDING OF AN A&E ALLOCATOR?

20   A.   An A&E allocator is an allocator that recognizes the contribution of each class

21        to the utility’s average demand, which is total annual kWh divided by 8,760

4         the A&E allocator differs from other allocators that have an energy component

5         in that it does not double count the energy portion of the allocator, which

6         otherwise punishes high load factor customers. Additionally, the A&E allocator

7         does not rely on fixed, subjective resource definitions. As such, even with its

8         use of energy as part of the allocator, the A&E allocator is, in Walmart’s

9         experience, an objective, transparent, and reasonable production plant cost

10        allocator, and would provide for some amount of energy allocation for the

12   Q.   HOW IS THE A&E ALLOCATOR CALCULATED?

13   A.   Mechanically, the CP or NCP peak demand value for each class is subdivided

14        into average demand and excess demand. The average demand, or energy

15        portion for each class, is weighted by the system load factor. The excess demand

16        portion, which is the difference between the average demand and the peak

17        demand for each class, is weighted by 1 minus the system load factor. As a

18        result, as system load factor increases and the system gets less peaky, the overall

19        weighting of the average demand portion of the allocator increases, and

20        conversely, as the system load factor decreases and the system gets more peaky,

21        the overall weighting of the excess demand portion of the allocator increases.
